newsitem.title: USA: Brazil sells $3 billion in bonds in break with past.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sells $3 billion in bonds in break with past.

text.p: In a bid to break from its debt-burdened past, Brazil Wednesday sold $3 billion in 30-year bonds and retired some of the expensive bonds that helped rescue it from the 1980s debt crisis.

The new bond attested to investors' belief that Brazil is shedding the stigma of its financially chaotic past. The new issue was not backed by U.S. Treasuries, as the retired debt was, showing that investors no longer demand the same high-quality guarantees to buy Brazilian securities.
The deal retired about $2.3 billion in Brady bonds, debt named for former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady that enabled the country to break out of a pattern of being in arrears.

The old Bradies were swapped for the new bonds, freeing $605 million of collateral backing them. Brazil's central bank said the new issue would save the country $150 million to $200 million over the life of the bonds.
"It is always good to retire restructured debt," Gustavo Franco, Brazilian Central Bank director for international affairs, told reporters in New York.
Brazilian officials cheered the deal, saying it showed global investors were confident Brazil could stand behind its own long-term paper.

Along with money saved, the bond swap will retire $2.7 billion of the nation's total $44 billion in Brady debt. But more important, analysts said, was the fact that investors jumped at the opportunity to buy long-term uncollateralized bonds from Brazil.
Only $750 million of the bond was offered for purchase outside of the swap, but a crush of investors tried to buy into it.

"We had over $16 billion in cash offers for the 30-year bond, which shows how interested investors were in the issue," said Linaldo Aguiar, head of the Brazilian Central Bank's foreign debt department.
At $3 billion, the issue was the second largest 30-year bond in the market after Italy's $3.5 billion issue, according to Brazil's Central Bank.
It also follows a credit upgrade earlier in the year by U.S. rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp. to BB-minus from B-plus, a move Brazilian officials said was long overdue.
Mexico carried out a similar Brady bond swap last year, but managed to sell only about $1.7 billion in new bonds.
Still, the deal was seen as the first step in a long-term plan to retire the Brady debt.
"This demand signals that there is further potential (for a swap), but that doesn't mean we would want to do something tomorrow," Aguiar said.
The bond came at an average 10.896 percent yield, priced at 93.234 with a coupon of 10.125 percent.
